claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was about ten feet long ("ten feet of stone man")
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man"

claims.claim: It was found behind a barn
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: Workers digging a well hit it on October 16, 1869
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant

claims.claim: The giant photograph is credited to Bain News Service and dated 1910
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher

claims.claim: The giant was photographed by Bain News Service in 1910
claims.quote: Author: Bain News Service, publisher

claims.claim: The print is a souvenir print
claims.quote: Title:  The  Onondaga giant

claims.claim: The print lists the figure's measurements
claims.quote: ITS DIMENSIONS ARE

claims.claim: Whole length of the figure was 10 feet 4½ inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: Length of nose, 6 inches
claims.quote: length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: Width of palm, 7 inches
claims.quote: width of palm, 7 inches

claims.claim: It weighed 2,990 pounds
claims.quote: The length of the giant was 10 feet 4+1⁄2 inches (3.162 m) and it weighed 2,990 pounds (1,360 kg).

claims.claim: The back of the stereocard names two men as the perpetrators
claims.quote: The perpetrators of the imposture are well remembered by old residents of Fort Dodge. Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: The stereocard was printed in 1873
claims.quote: Date: 1873

claims.claim: The stereocard verso says the block was taken from this quarry to Chicago, the giant carved, then shipped to New York, buried in a barn lot and subsequently "discovered"
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name, where it was buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered".

claims.claim: The stereocard is from the New York Public Library
claims.quote: File:View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa (NYPL b11707469-G90F191 001B).tiff

claims.claim: The giant started as a block of gypsum in Iowa
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: In 1868 Hull hired men at Fort Dodge to quarry a block ten feet four and a half inches long
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: Hull told the quarrymen the block was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh said gypsum buried for centuries in wet earth could not keep fresh tool marks
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did)

claims.claim: Marsh called the giant "a most decided humbug"
claims.quote: termed it "a most decided humbug"

claims.claim: Hull confessed to the press on December 10, 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: On February 2, 1870, both his giant and Barnum's copy were ruled fakes in court
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: Hull confessed proudly rather than under pressure of criticism
claims.quote: Hull proclaimed that he did not confess because of the pressing criticism, but confessed proudly that he intended for the hoax to be exposed

claims.claim: It is unresolved whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what the job was for
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: The Chicago stonecutter who took the job was named Edward Burkhardt
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was not real; it was carved in 1868
claims.quote: During November 1868, Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell.

claims.claim: The barn was William C. Newell's, in Cardiff, New York
claims.quote: behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: Newell put a tent over the giant
claims.quote: The next day, a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant.

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing
claims.quote: Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people a day came
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day as the demand for wagons and carriages dramatically increased.

claims.claim: The town's hotels and restaurants had their best four days ever
claims.quote: The hotels and restaurants in Cardiff saw more customers in those four days than they had ever seen before.

claims.claim: George Hull was Newell's cousin and a tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival about the giants in Genesis 6:4
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: The giant was carved in Chicago in the shape of Hull's own body
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: Hull left off the hair because a geologist told him hair does not petrify
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles were used to age the surface and simulate pores
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores. The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: The hoax cost $2,600
claims.quote: By then, he had spent US$2,600 (equivalent to $63,000 in 2025) for the hoax.

claims.claim: Barnum's copy was an unauthorized plaster copy
claims.quote: he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy

claims.claim: "There's a sucker born every minute" was said by David Hannum, head of the syndicate, not Barnum, and the misattribution persists
claims.quote: David Hannum was quoted as saying, "There's a sucker born every minute" in reference to spectators paying to see Barnum's giant. Since then, the quotation has often been misattributed to Barnum himself.

claims.claim: The 1873 stereocard shows the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry
claims.quote: VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN. NEAR FORT DODGE.IOWA. This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: The lithograph is titled "The Onondaga Giant"
claims.quote: THE ONONDAGA GIANT.
